analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin copays at $35 a month for Medicare and private health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate vote: after introduction it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended, despite 37 Senate sponsors and cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would limit what people with diabetes pay out of pocket for insulin. Medicare Part D plans could not charge more than $35 for a month's supply of insulin, starting in late 2022, and private and employer plans could not charge more than $35 a month (or 25% of the drug's negotiated price after rebates, if that is lower) starting in 2023. It also bars plans from applying their deductible to insulin, and requires plans to cover at least one insulin of each type and dosage form, so no one is left hunting for a covered version of the insulin they use. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use insulin and are covered by Medicare Part D, employer plans, or individual health insurance. For them, the bill would replace unpredictable, sometimes hundreds-of-dollars monthly insulin costs with a flat $35 cap and no deductible. People who currently skip or ration insulin doses because of cost would benefit most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insulin users on Medicare or private plans

how_it_helps.text: Caps Medicare Part D cost-sharing for a month's supply of covered insulin at $35 beginning October 1, 2022, and prevents the Part D deductible from applying to insulin [S2, S3].

Caps cost-sharing under group health plans and private insurance at $35 per 30-day supply, or 25% of the insulin's negotiated price net of rebates if lower, beginning in 2023, with no deductible applied to insulin [S2, S3].

Requires plans to cover at least one insulin product of each dosage form (vial, pump, inhaler) and each type (rapid-acting, long-acting, premixed, etc.), so users of less common insulins are not left with unaffordable alternatives [S3].
Requires that insulin cost-sharing payments count toward the plan's deductible and out-of-pocket maximum [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor plans would absorb the difference between what patients pay and insulin's full cost, likely passing some of it into premiums. The bill does not touch the list prices insulin manufacturers charge, so their revenue is largely protected.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers sponsoring plans

drawbacks.text: The bill caps what patients pay, not what insulin costs; the gap is shifted to insurers and plan sponsors and can resurface in premiums rather than lowering the underlying price of the drug [S2, S3].

The private-plan cap applies only to a plan's 'selected' insulin products — one per type and dosage form — and plans may still charge more for other insulin products or for insulin from out-of-network providers [S3].
Insulin manufacturers' pricing is left untouched, so the structural driver of high insulin costs — list prices set well above production cost — remains in place [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insulin users, the benefit is concrete and immediate: a hard $35 monthly cap with no deductible is the difference between filling a prescription and rationing it. The honest cost is that the bill moves the money rather than eliminating it — insurers and employers absorb the difference, which flows into premiums. And because it never touches manufacturer list prices, it treats the symptom. A stronger bill would pair the copay cap with pressure on the drugmakers' prices; this one, as written, asks payers and patients' plans to carry the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2022 and referred straight to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a vote on it; when the Congress ended in January 2023, the bill died there.

narrative.text: Sen. Raphael Warnock introduced the Affordable Insulin Now Act on February 17, 2022 [S1].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, its only action in the chamber [S5].
37 senators backed it — sponsor Warnock plus 36 cosponsors, 35 Democrats and one independent [S4].
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action followed before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers keep their list prices unchallenged, and insurers and pharmacy benefit managers avoid absorbing the $35 cap's cost. Insulin users keep paying whatever their plans charge, including high deductible-phase costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drugmakers, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers

for.name: Sen. Raphael Warnock
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 36 Senate cosponsors for it.

for.name: 35 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, plus one independent senator, giving it majority-caucus backing.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but his committee never took it up — no markup or vote was scheduled in the nine months after referral.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but never brought it to the Senate floor for a vote.

against.name: 43 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against the identical $35 cap on private-insurance insulin copays when it came to the Senate floor as an amendment in August 2022, leaving it short of the 60 votes needed to advance (57-43).

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself never reached a vote, but when the same $35 private-insurance cap came to the Senate floor in August 2022 attached to the Inflation Reduction Act, it drew 57 votes including 3 Republicans and fell short of the 60 needed — while 35 of 48 Democratic senators had cosponsored this standalone version.

industries.note: The bill forces group, individual, and Medicare Part D plans to absorb insulin costs above the $35 cap and skip the deductible on insulin, likely recouped through premiums. Insurers' interest in the status quo runs against insulin users who need the cap.

The cap is computed on the insulin's price net of all rebates, including rebates retained by middlemen like PBMs, exposing their take in the pricing chain and shrinking the spread they earn. PBMs have a stake in keeping current cost-sharing structures unchanged.

The bill caps what patients and payers pay at the pharmacy but never caps what manufacturers charge, leaving the list prices that made insulin unaffordable fully intact. Under this bill the drugmakers' revenue and pricing power are locked in even as patients get relief.

The bill amends ERISA to require employer plans to cover selected insulin products at no more than $35 per month without a deductible, a new benefit mandate for large employers that many would pass into employee premiums.
